items.prompt: Ravi and Ines got the exact same fluent, confident AI answer about honey. What does the fact that it was wrong tell you about fluency and confidence in an AI's answer?
choices: Fluency and confidence are strong evidence the answer was checked against a real source
Fluency and confidence are properties of how the text was generated, not evidence the claim is true
An AI can only sound confident when it's actually correct
Fluent answers are wrong more often than hesitant-sounding ones
items.explanation: An AI's fluency and confidence come from how the text was generated (predicting plausible next words), not from a step where the claim was verified against reality. A wrong answer and a right one can be delivered with identical smoothness and certainty in tone — so neither is a signal you can use to tell them apart.
items.reference:
The claim: "Fluent and confident" only describes the surface of an answer, not whether it was checked.

Why: An AI is optimized to produce plausible-sounding text, not verified-true text — so tone tells you nothing about correctness.

items.prompt: An AI assistant answers a factual question with a specific number, a confident tone, and no hedging language anywhere in the response. On its own, what does that tell you about whether the number is correct?
choices: Nothing reliable — confidence and specificity are not the same as verification
It's almost certainly correct, since a wrong answer would usually include hedging
It means the AI checked the number against a live source before answering
It's more trustworthy than an answer that hedges or expresses uncertainty
items.explanation: Nothing about the confidence or specificity of the wording is produced by a fact-checking step — both are just features of the generated text. A wrong number can be stated with exactly as much confidence as a right one.
items.reference:
The claim: "Fluent and confident" only describes the surface of an answer, not whether it was checked.

Why: An AI is optimized to produce plausible-sounding text, not verified-true text — so tone tells you nothing about correctness.

items.prompt: Someone says: "The AI's answer was so detailed and specific, it had to be based on real research." What's the flaw in that reasoning?
choices: There's no flaw — detail and specificity are reliable signs an answer is grounded in real research
Detail and specificity describe how the text reads, and can be generated whether or not the underlying claim is true
Detailed answers are actually less trustworthy than short ones
AI assistants are incapable of producing detailed wrong answers
items.explanation: Detail and specificity are qualities of the generated wording, not proof of a verification step behind it. A wrong claim can be just as richly detailed as a correct one — the honey answer in this unit's scenario was highly specific and still wrong.
items.reference:
The claim: "Fluent and confident" only describes the surface of an answer, not whether it was checked.

Why: An AI is optimized to produce plausible-sounding text, not verified-true text — so tone tells you nothing about correctness.

items.prompt: Ravi and Ines received the identical wrong AI answer. What actually caused their outcomes to differ?
choices: Ines asked the AI a more carefully worded question than Ravi did
Ines happened to already know the correct fact about honey and infants
Ines had a habit of checking one specific claim against an independent source before acting on it
The AI gave Ines a different, more accurate answer than it gave Ravi
items.explanation: Both received the exact same wrong answer, worded identically. The only difference was Ines's habit of checking the one claim her decision actually depended on before acting — not better phrasing, not prior expertise, and not a different AI response.
items.reference:
The claim: Same question, same AI, same wrong answer — different outcomes.

Why: The one difference was a verification habit applied before acting, not who asked a better question or knew more.

items.prompt: In the honey scenario, was the AI's answer different for Ravi than for Ines?
choices: Yes — the AI gave Ravi a wrong answer and Ines a correct one
No — both received the exact same wrong answer; only what happened after differed
Yes — Ines's question was phrased differently, producing a better answer
No information is given about whether the answers matched
items.explanation: The scenario states both received the identical wrong answer, word for word. What changed the outcome was entirely what happened between reading the answer and acting on it, not the answer itself.
items.reference:
The claim: Same question, same AI, same wrong answer — different outcomes.

Why: The one difference was a verification habit applied before acting, not who asked a better question or knew more.

items.prompt: What does the fact that Ines and Ravi got an identical wrong answer, with different real-world outcomes, mainly demonstrate?
choices: That AI answers are randomized, so the same question can produce different results
That the outcome depended on a habit applied after the answer arrived, not on the answer itself
That Ravi's AI assistant was a lower-quality tool than Ines's
That the honey question was ambiguous enough to have two valid answers
items.explanation: The scenario is built so the input (question and answer) is held identical on purpose — this isolates the one variable that actually mattered: whether a verification habit was applied before the answer became something acted on.
items.reference:
The claim: Same question, same AI, same wrong answer — different outcomes.

Why: The one difference was a verification habit applied before acting, not who asked a better question or knew more.

items.prompt: According to the verification habit described in this unit, which of these AI-provided claims deserves the most scrutiny before you act on it?
choices: The AI's guess at what year a minor historical event happened, out of idle curiosity
The AI's claim about whether a food is safe for an infant, right before you serve it
The AI's suggestion for a synonym while you're casually drafting a text message
The AI's estimate of how many countries exist in a particular region
items.explanation: The habit scales scrutiny to stakes: a claim a real, consequential decision is about to rest on — like a food-safety judgment about to be acted on immediately — deserves a check. Low-stakes curiosity questions with nothing riding on them don't need the same treatment.
items.reference:
The claim: Not every AI claim needs the same level of scrutiny.

Why: Scale the check to the stakes — load-bearing or surprising claims earn a check; passing details usually don't.

items.prompt: What makes a claim "load-bearing" in the sense this unit uses the term?
choices: It's the longest or most detailed sentence in the AI's answer
A real decision or later reasoning will actually rest on it
It's the first claim the AI states in its response
It happens to be the claim the reader finds most interesting
items.explanation: A load-bearing claim is one an actual decision depends on — if it's wrong, something real changes as a result. That's what separates it from a passing detail that wouldn't change what you do even if it turned out to be false.
items.reference:
The claim: Not every AI claim needs the same level of scrutiny.

Why: Scale the check to the stakes — load-bearing or surprising claims earn a check; passing details usually don't.

items.prompt: Someone argues that a genuine verification habit means fact-checking every single sentence an AI ever produces, with equal effort each time. Is that what this unit describes?
choices: Yes — anything less than checking every sentence is a lapse in the habit
No — the habit is scaling scrutiny to how load-bearing or surprising a specific claim is, not checking everything equally
No — the habit means never trusting an AI answer under any circumstance
Yes, but only for claims longer than one sentence
items.explanation: Checking everything with equal intensity isn't sustainable and isn't the point — the skill is identifying which specific claims are load-bearing or surprising and directing the check there, leaving low-stakes details unchecked.
items.reference:
The claim: Not every AI claim needs the same level of scrutiny.

Why: Scale the check to the stakes — load-bearing or surprising claims earn a check; passing details usually don't.

items.prompt: Which best describes a "verification habit" as this unit defines it?
choices: A one-time decision to be generally skeptical of AI tools
A small, repeatable check performed on a specific claim before treating it as true
Refusing to use AI tools for anything factual
Asking the AI the same question twice and comparing the two answers
items.explanation: The habit is a repeatable, specific action — checking one particular claim against an independent source — not a vague general attitude, and not avoidance of AI tools altogether.
items.reference:
The claim: A verification habit is a specific, repeatable action, not a vague attitude.

Why: "Be more skeptical in general" doesn't catch a specific wrong claim the way "check this one claim against an independent source" does.

items.prompt: Ines checks the AI's honey claim against her pediatrician's page. What made this an example of a verification habit, rather than just luck?
choices: She happened to already have the pediatrician's page bookmarked
It was a deliberate, specific, repeatable action she takes before acting on this kind of claim, not a one-off coincidence
The AI told her to double-check its own answer
She waited a few days before deciding what to do
items.explanation: What makes it a habit rather than luck is that it's the kind of specific, deliberate check she'd apply to any similarly load-bearing claim, not something that happened to occur to her once in this particular case.
items.reference:
The claim: A verification habit is a specific, repeatable action, not a vague attitude.

Why: "Be more skeptical in general" doesn't catch a specific wrong claim the way "check this one claim against an independent source" does.

items.prompt: How is a wrong AI answer typically different from a poorly-sourced blog post making the same wrong claim?
choices: The AI answer is usually less specific and less confident than the blog post
The AI answer carries none of the usual visible warning signs (no author, no citations, sketchy layout) that a shaky article tends to signal
AI answers are always accompanied by a visible confidence score
There's no meaningful difference between the two
items.explanation: A shaky article often signals its own unreliability through visible tells — missing author, no citations, poor presentation. An AI's wrong answer is grammatically perfect, specific, and personalized to the exact question, with none of those tells, which is exactly what makes it a distinct and newer risk.
items.reference:
The claim: A wrong AI answer often reads more authoritative than a shaky article, not less.

Why: Missing the usual reliability tells (author, citations, sourcing) is exactly what makes an AI's confident wrongness harder to spot than a poorly-sourced article's.

items.prompt: Why does this unit describe an AI's confidently wrong answer as a genuinely new kind of risk, rather than just the same old problem of untrustworthy information sources?
choices: Because AI tools are newer technology than websites
Because it's generated fresh and personalized to your exact question, and lacks the visible unreliability signals an older, static bad source usually shows
Because AI answers are always longer than articles
Because AI tools cannot be fact-checked at all
items.explanation: The novelty isn't the technology's age — it's that the answer is generated on the spot for your specific question and delivered with none of the usual tells (no missing author, no absent citations, no sketchy presentation) that make a bad static source easier to spot.
items.reference:
The claim: A wrong AI answer often reads more authoritative than a shaky article, not less.

Why: Missing the usual reliability tells (author, citations, sourcing) is exactly what makes an AI's confident wrongness harder to spot than a poorly-sourced article's.

items.prompt: In plain terms, what is a large language model actually optimized to produce when it answers a question?
choices: The most statistically plausible next words, given the text so far
A claim that has been checked against a current, authoritative source
The shortest possible correct answer
A response ranked by a panel of human fact-checkers before being shown
items.explanation: The generation process predicts plausible continuations of text based on patterns in what it was trained on. That process usually lines up with accurate answers, since most writing about a topic tends to be roughly correct — but nothing in it checks a specific claim against a current source before the words are produced.
items.reference:
The claim: Plausible next words, not verified facts, is what the generation process actually optimizes for.

Why: Most training text is roughly accurate, so plausible and true usually align — but there's no built-in check confirming they do for any given answer.

items.prompt: Why do plausible-sounding AI answers usually turn out to be accurate, even though nothing directly checks them against a source?
choices: Because AI models have a built-in fact-checking step run before every answer
Because most of the writing the model learned from tends to be roughly accurate, so plausible wording and true content usually coincide
Because wrong answers are automatically filtered out before being shown
Because the model only answers questions it has explicitly verified
items.explanation: The alignment between plausible and true is a byproduct of most training text being roughly accurate — not the result of any verification step. That's exactly why it's not reliable for the cases where it breaks down.
items.reference:
The claim: Plausible next words, not verified facts, is what the generation process actually optimizes for.

Why: Most training text is roughly accurate, so plausible and true usually align — but there's no built-in check confirming they do for any given answer.

items.prompt: The honey answer in this unit's scenario was wrong. Given how the generation process works, what most likely explains why?
choices: The model deliberately chose to mislead the user
It produced the most plausible-sounding completion for that question, and that happened to land on an outdated or incorrect version of the fact
The model ran a verification step that returned an incorrect result
The question was too short for the model to answer accurately
items.explanation: There's no deception or verification failure involved — the process simply generated the most statistically plausible-sounding completion, and in this case that completion matched an outdated or incorrect version of the fact rather than the current, correct one.
items.reference:
The claim: Plausible next words, not verified facts, is what the generation process actually optimizes for.

Why: Most training text is roughly accurate, so plausible and true usually align — but there's no built-in check confirming they do for any given answer.

items.prompt: In the two loops diagram, what is the single decision point that separates the outsourcing-understanding trap from the AI-as-accelerant loop?
choices: Which AI tool was used to generate the answer
Whether a load-bearing or surprising claim gets checked against an independent source before becoming belief
How long the AI's answer is
Whether the question was asked out loud or typed
items.explanation: Both loops start identically — ask a question, get a fluent answer. The fork is entirely about what happens next: whether the load-bearing claim gets an independent check before it becomes something believed and acted on.
items.reference:
The claim: Both loops start the same way; only the check-before-belief step differs.

Why: The accelerant loop keeps the AI's speed but adds back the one step the trap skips — an independent check on what matters.

items.prompt: Does the AI-as-accelerant loop mean giving up the speed benefit of using an AI tool?
choices: Yes — it requires researching everything from scratch without any AI involvement
No — it still uses the AI for a fast first draft of an answer; it adds one independent check on the load-bearing claim before that answer becomes belief
Yes — it means verifying every single sentence the AI produces, which is slower than not using AI at all
No — it requires no additional steps beyond what the outsourcing-understanding trap does
items.explanation: The accelerant loop keeps the speed advantage of getting a fast draft answer from the AI. What it adds is a single, targeted independent check on the specific claim that's load-bearing — not a full from-scratch re-derivation of everything.
items.reference:
The claim: Both loops start the same way; only the check-before-belief step differs.

Why: The accelerant loop keeps the AI's speed but adds back the one step the trap skips — an independent check on what matters.

items.prompt: In the outsourcing-understanding trap, what specifically happens to an unverified claim over time?
choices: It's automatically discarded after a short period
It quietly becomes part of what the person believes and acts on, without ever having been checked
It gets flagged by the AI tool itself as unverified
It's replaced by a corrected version the next time the AI is asked
items.explanation: Without a check, an accepted claim doesn't stay clearly labeled as "unverified" in the person's mind — it settles into ordinary belief, indistinguishable from things that actually were confirmed, which is exactly what makes the trap dangerous over time.
items.reference:
The claim: Both loops start the same way; only the check-before-belief step differs.

Why: The accelerant loop keeps the AI's speed but adds back the one step the trap skips — an independent check on what matters.

items.prompt: An AI answer includes the phrase "according to official guidelines..." Does naming a source like this mean the claim has been verified?
choices: Yes — naming a source is itself proof the claim was checked against it
No — a named source is still generated text and needs to actually be opened and compared against the claim
Yes, but only if the source is named more than once
No — AI tools are never able to reference real sources
items.explanation: A source name in an AI's answer is produced by the same plausible-text-generation process as everything else in the response — it isn't proof that source was actually consulted or that it says what the AI claims it says. The check is opening the source and comparing it directly.
items.reference:
The claim: A cited-sounding answer is a pointer to check, not proof already delivered.

Why: Naming a source is still just more generated text — the verification step is opening it and comparing it to the claim.

items.prompt: What's the actual verification step once an AI answer names a specific source for a claim?
choices: Treating the citation as sufficient and moving on
Opening the named source directly and confirming it actually says what the AI claimed it says
Asking the AI a second time to see if it names the same source again
Assuming the citation is accurate because it sounds specific
items.explanation: The only way a citation becomes real verification is by actually opening it and checking that it supports the claim as stated — repeating the question or trusting the citation's presence alone skips the step that matters.
items.reference:
The claim: A cited-sounding answer is a pointer to check, not proof already delivered.

Why: Naming a source is still just more generated text — the verification step is opening it and comparing it to the claim.

items.prompt: According to the habit described in this unit, which factor should most increase how carefully a specific AI claim gets checked?
choices: How long the AI took to generate the answer
How surprising the claim is, or how much a real decision depends on it
How many words the answer contains
Whether the answer includes an emoji or friendly tone
items.explanation: The habit scales scrutiny to how surprising a claim is (something you'd have bet against) or how load-bearing it is (a real decision rests on it) — not to surface features like length or tone, which say nothing about correctness.
items.reference:
The claim: Surprising or load-bearing claims earn extra scrutiny; routine ones usually don't need it.

Why: A claim you'd have bet against, or one a real decision rests on, is exactly where being wrong costs the most.

items.prompt: An AI claim matches exactly what you already expected to hear, and nothing real depends on it either way. Does the verification habit call for the same level of scrutiny here as for a surprising, high-stakes claim?
choices: Yes — every claim deserves identical scrutiny regardless of context
No — scrutiny is meant to scale up for surprising or load-bearing claims, and this one is neither
Yes, because unexpected claims are always false and expected claims are always true
No — expected claims should actually get more scrutiny than surprising ones
items.explanation: The whole point of scaling scrutiny is that not every claim needs equal treatment. A claim that matches expectations and has nothing riding on it is a reasonable place to spend less effort checking, freeing that effort for claims that are surprising or load-bearing.
items.reference:
The claim: Surprising or load-bearing claims earn extra scrutiny; routine ones usually don't need it.

Why: A claim you'd have bet against, or one a real decision rests on, is exactly where being wrong costs the most.

items.prompt: Per the passive-vs-active comparison, what happens to an unverified claim under passive acceptance, a month later?
choices: It's automatically forgotten because it was never checked
It quietly becomes 'something I know,' indistinguishable from claims that actually were verified
It gets flagged in memory as uncertain forever
It's replaced by whatever the AI says the next time it's asked
items.explanation: Under passive acceptance, an unverified claim doesn't stay tagged as 'unchecked' — over time it blends into ordinary belief just like anything else, with no visible marker distinguishing it from something that was actually confirmed.
items.reference:
The claim: Passive acceptance and active verification diverge at the exact same three moments — right after the answer, on a surprising/high-stakes claim, and when a source is cited.

Why: Only checked claims should graduate into confident belief; unchecked ones should stay visibly tentative.

items.prompt: In the active-verification column, what's the immediate status of an AI's answer right after it's received, before any check happens?
choices: Settled fact, ready to act on
A draft claim, not yet treated as fact
Automatically discarded until independently reproduced twice
Assumed false until proven otherwise
items.explanation: The active-verification mindset treats a fresh AI answer as a draft claim — plausible, worth taking seriously, but not yet promoted to "fact" until the load-bearing part of it has actually been checked.
items.reference:
The claim: Passive acceptance and active verification diverge at the exact same three moments — right after the answer, on a surprising/high-stakes claim, and when a source is cited.

Why: Only checked claims should graduate into confident belief; unchecked ones should stay visibly tentative.

items.prompt: What is the practical difference between the passive and active columns when the AI's answer includes a cited source or stated reasoning?
choices: Passive treats the citation's presence as proof; active opens the source and compares it to the claim
There is no difference — both treat a citation the same way
Active ignores citations entirely, treating them as noise
Passive always rejects cited answers as suspicious
items.explanation: The table draws exactly this line: passive acceptance treats a citation's mere presence as if it settles the matter, while active verification treats the citation as a pointer and actually opens it to confirm it supports the claim.
items.reference:
The claim: Passive acceptance and active verification diverge at the exact same three moments — right after the answer, on a surprising/high-stakes claim, and when a source is cited.

Why: Only checked claims should graduate into confident belief; unchecked ones should stay visibly tentative.

items.prompt: In the step-by-step walkthrough of Ines's check, why did she open her pediatrician's own patient page instead of asking the same AI the same question again, worded differently?
choices: Asking the same model again would likely still produce a similarly plausible-sounding answer for the same underlying reason — it isn't an independent check
Asking again is technically impossible with most AI assistants
Rewording a question to the same AI always produces the opposite answer
She didn't have time to type a second question
items.explanation: Re-asking the same model isn't an independent check — the same generation process that produced the wrong answer the first time is liable to produce a similarly plausible-sounding (and possibly still wrong) answer again. A genuinely independent, authoritative source is what actually tests the claim.
items.reference:
The claim: Ines's check worked because it used a genuinely independent, authoritative source — not a second AI query.

Why: Re-asking the same model risks reproducing the same plausible-but-wrong answer; an independent source actually tests the claim.

items.prompt: The AI's honey answer contained several claims — an age threshold, a safety judgment, and a general note about common practice. Which one did Ines actually verify, and why?
choices: All of them equally, because thoroughness means checking every claim in an answer
Only the age/safety threshold, because that's the one claim her decision that night actually depended on
Only the note about common practice, because it was the most surprising part
None of them — she based her decision on general caution alone, without checking any specific claim
items.explanation: Ines isolated the one load-bearing claim — whether 8 months was old enough — and checked that specifically. The rest of the answer's color (how honey is described, general practice) didn't change her decision either way, so it didn't need the same scrutiny.
items.reference:
The claim: Ines's check worked because it used a genuinely independent, authoritative source — not a second AI query.

Why: Re-asking the same model risks reproducing the same plausible-but-wrong answer; an independent source actually tests the claim.

items.prompt: After finding the discrepancy between the AI's claim and her pediatrician's page, what was the final step Ines took to fully close the loop?
choices: Nothing further — skipping the honey was sufficient on its own
She called the pediatrician's office the next morning to ask what to introduce instead
She reported the AI's error to the company that made it
She asked the same AI to explain why it had been wrong
items.explanation: Skipping the honey addressed the immediate risk, but calling the office the next morning is what actually closed the loop — turning a caught error into a concrete next step, rather than leaving a gap (what should be served instead) unresolved.
items.reference:
The claim: Ines's check worked because it used a genuinely independent, authoritative source — not a second AI query.

Why: Re-asking the same model risks reproducing the same plausible-but-wrong answer; an independent source actually tests the claim.

items.prompt: In the sort-complexity example, the AI claimed Python's built-in `list.sort()` runs in O(n) time. What's actually true, and what kind of check exposes the error?
choices: It's actually O(n log n) — exposed by checking official documentation or timing sorts of increasing size and seeing time grow faster than linearly
The AI was correct, and no further check was needed
It's actually O(n^2) — exposed only by reading the sorting algorithm's full source code
The claim can't be checked without a computer science degree
items.explanation: Python's built-in sort (Timsort) runs in O(n log n) time on average and worst case, not O(n). This can be confirmed either by consulting the language's own official documentation or by running a small experiment — timing sorts on lists of increasing size and observing the running time grows faster than a straight line — neither of which requires being a specialist.
items.reference:
The claim: A highly technical claim (sort complexity) still has checks anyone can run — they just take longer than the honey example's single page.

Why: Official documentation or a small timed experiment both settle the claim without requiring specialist background.

items.prompt: Why is the sort-complexity example harder to verify than the honey claim, even though both are checkable by a non-specialist?
choices: Because the sort-complexity claim requires paid access to verify
Because there usually isn't one single obvious page to read and immediately settle it — the check takes longer and requires knowing where to look or how to test it
Because programming claims can never be independently verified
Because the honey claim was actually harder to check, not easier
items.explanation: Unlike the honey claim's one clearly authoritative page, verifying a sort's time complexity usually means consulting official documentation (which requires knowing where to look) or running a small experiment — still doable by a non-specialist, but slower and less immediately obvious than opening one page.
items.reference:
The claim: A highly technical claim (sort complexity) still has checks anyone can run — they just take longer than the honey example's single page.

Why: Official documentation or a small timed experiment both settle the claim without requiring specialist background.

items.prompt: Per the comparison table, what should you do with a highly technical or specialized claim that you genuinely can't verify given the time and resources available?
choices: Treat it as true anyway, since the AI sounded confident
Explicitly flag the claim as unverified before it becomes load-bearing elsewhere
Discard the entire conversation and start over with a different AI tool
Assume it's false until a specialist happens to confirm it
items.explanation: When a genuine check isn't feasible in the time available, the honest move is to flag the claim explicitly as unverified rather than let it quietly become the foundation for something else — the same principle as the speed-vs-certainty section's advice under time pressure.
items.reference:
The claim: A single check often fully settles an easy claim but only narrows a technical one — a second check adds real value there.

Why: The habit doesn't change with difficulty; how much a single check can be trusted to settle it does.

items.prompt: For a highly technical or specialized claim, how much should one check typically be trusted to settle the matter, compared to an easily checkable claim like the honey example?
choices: Exactly the same — one check settles any claim regardless of how technical it is
Often less — a single check may only narrow it, and a second independent check can add real additional value
More — technical claims are actually easier to fully settle than everyday ones
None at all — technical claims can never meaningfully be checked by a non-specialist
items.explanation: The comparison table draws exactly this distinction: the honey claim was usually settled outright by one authoritative page, while a highly technical claim may only be narrowed by a single check, making a second independent check genuinely more valuable there than it would be for an easy claim.
items.reference:
The claim: A single check often fully settles an easy claim but only narrows a technical one — a second check adds real value there.

Why: The habit doesn't change with difficulty; how much a single check can be trusted to settle it does.

items.prompt: Does the core verification habit itself change between an easily checkable claim and a highly technical one?
choices: Yes — technical claims don't need to be checked at all, since no one but a specialist could understand the answer
No — the habit (check the load-bearing claim before it becomes belief) stays the same; what changes is how much effort finding the right kind of check takes
Yes — easily checkable claims should be trusted without any check, while technical ones always need several
No — but only because AI tools are equally reliable on both kinds of claims
items.explanation: The underlying habit is constant: check the load-bearing claim before it becomes belief. What changes across the two examples is how much a single check can be trusted to settle things, and how much work it takes to find and run the appropriate check.
items.reference:
The claim: A single check often fully settles an easy claim but only narrows a technical one — a second check adds real value there.

Why: The habit doesn't change with difficulty; how much a single check can be trusted to settle it does.

items.prompt: Under real time pressure, when a full verification check genuinely isn't possible, what does this unit recommend instead of skipping verification entirely and presenting the claim as settled?
choices: Repeat the AI's claim with full confidence anyway, since there's no time to do otherwise
Run whatever fast, partial check is possible, and explicitly flag what wasn't verified rather than presenting it as settled fact
Refuse to state any claim at all until it can be fully verified, regardless of the cost of delay
Ask a colleague to vouch for the claim without them checking it either
items.explanation: Time pressure is a reason to shrink the check, not skip flagging that it didn't happen. A fast, partial check plus an honest "this hasn't been confirmed" is a fundamentally different, more honest position than presenting an unverified claim with full confidence.
items.reference:
The claim: Time pressure compresses the check; it doesn't excuse presenting an unverified claim as settled.

Why: A lucky correct outcome doesn't retroactively make skipping the flag the right call — it's still a gamble that happened to pay off.

items.prompt: A colleague repeats an unverified AI claim in a meeting under time pressure without flagging it, and the claim turns out to be correct. Does that outcome validate the decision not to flag it?
choices: Yes — a correct outcome proves the shortcut was safe to take
No — being right that time was luck, not evidence the unflagged shortcut is safe to repeat
Yes, but only if the claim was later independently confirmed by someone else
No — the claim should have been treated as false regardless of the outcome
items.explanation: An unverified claim being correct once doesn't mean the process behind stating it as settled fact was sound. The risk was that anyone hearing it had no way to distinguish checked claims from unchecked ones — next time the unverified claim might not get lucky.
items.reference:
The claim: Time pressure compresses the check; it doesn't excuse presenting an unverified claim as settled.

Why: A lucky correct outcome doesn't retroactively make skipping the flag the right call — it's still a gamble that happened to pay off.

items.prompt: Does time pressure eliminate the verification habit described in this unit, or change its form?
choices: It eliminates it entirely — under time pressure, there is no reasonable version of the habit to apply
It changes its form — the check compresses and any unverified part gets explicitly flagged, rather than disappearing silently
It has no effect at all — the exact same lengthy check should be run regardless of time available
It reverses the habit — time pressure means claims should be treated as more trustworthy, not less
items.explanation: Time pressure doesn't remove the habit — it compresses the check into whatever is feasible in the time available, and makes explicit flagging of what wasn't verified even more important, since presenting an unverified claim as settled becomes more tempting exactly when there's less time to catch the mistake.
items.reference:
